Upper bounds on the average edit distance between two random strings

**Abstract**

We study the average edit distance between two random strings. More precisely, we adapt a technique introduced by Lueker in the context of the average longest common subsequence of two random strings to improve the known upper bound on the average edit distance. We improve all the known upper bounds for small alphabets. We also provide a new implementation of Lueker technique to improve the lower bound on the average length of the longest common subsequence of two random strings for all small alphabets of size other than 2 and 4.

## 1 Introduction

We consider two different notions of similarity between pairs of strings. The first notion is the _length of the longest common subsequence_ between two strings _u_, and _v_, denoted by LCS(_u,v_). The second notion is the edit distance (also called Levenshtein distance) between two strings _u_, and _v_, denoted by _d<sub>e</sub>(u,v_), which is the minimum number of substitutions, deletions and insertions necessary to transform _u_ to _v_.

In particular, we are interested in the average edit distance denoted _e<sub>k</sub>(n_) (resp. average length of the longest common subsequence denoted \(\ell_k(n)\)) between two random _k_-ary strings of length _n_. More precisely, we provide bounds on the two following quantities whose existence is implied by Fekete’s Lemma

\(\alpha_k=lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{e_k(n)}{n}\text{and}\gamma_k=lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\ell_k(n)}{n}.\)

The so called Chvátal-Sankoff constant \(\gamma_2\), and the other \(\gamma_k\) received a lot of attention since 1975 [1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 8, 7, 9, 13, 18, ...]. In particular, we know that \(\gamma_2\) is algebraic [18] and that \(0.788071\le\gamma_2\le 0.826280\) [14]. Until recently the best bounds on \(\gamma_k\) for other small values of _k_ were given in [12]. A few days before the publication of the present article on the arXiv another preprint improved most of the bounds known for \(\gamma_k\) and variant of \(\gamma_k\) that consider the expected LCS of _t_ random strings [11]. In particular, they proved \(\gamma_2\ge 0.792665\) We improve on all the bounds for \(\gamma_k\) given by [11] other than \(\gamma_2\) and \(\gamma_4\) where we only beat the previous best bound by Lueker [14].

Matthieu Rosenfeld

LIRMM, Univ Montpellier, CNRS, Montpellier, France

July 26, 2024

arXiv:2407.18113v1 [math.CO] 25 Jul 2024

## 2 Average edit distance

For any strings _u,v_, _d<sub>e</sub>(u,v_) is the _edit distance_ (or _Levenshtein distance_) between _u_ and _v_, that is, the minimum number of substitutions, deletions and insertions necessary to transform _u_ to _v_. Given two strings \(u,v\in\mathcal{A}^*\), and letters \(a,b\in\mathcal{A}\), we have<tbc>

\(d_e(au,bv)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
d_e(u,v) & \text{if}a=b \\
1+min(d_e(u,v),d_e(u,bv),d_e(au,v)) & \text{otherwise}
\end{array}\right.\) (1)

<tbc>and for all _u_, \(d_e(u,\varepsilon)=d_e(\varepsilon,u)=|u|\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the empty string. For any strings \(u,v,u',v'\), we have<tbc>

\(d_e(uv,u'v')\le d_e(u,u')+d_e(v,v').\) (2)

<tbc>For any _n_, we let _U<sub>n,k</sub>=d<sub>e</sub>(X_<sub>1</sub>_...X<sub>n</sub>,Y_<sub>1</sub>_...,Y<sub>n</sub>_) where the _X<sub>i</sub>_ and _Y<sub>i</sub>_ are taken uniformly at random from A={1_,...,k_}. For all _k_, the quantity \(\alpha_k\) is defined as

\(\alpha_k=lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[d_e(X_1\dots X_n,Y_1\dots Y_n)\right]}{n}=lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{U_{n,k}}{n}.\)

Linearity of expectation and equation (2) imply that the sequence \(\left(\mathbb{E}\left[U_{n,k}\right]\right)_{n\ge 1}\) is subadditive. Thus by Feketes’s lemma, \(\alpha_k\) is well-defined.

Since we will always be working with one specific ambient alphabet A, we omit the _k_, and, from now on, we write for instance _U<sub>n</sub>_ instead of _U<sub>n,k</sub>_. Similarly, in the following the _X<sub>i</sub>_ and _Y<sub>i</sub>_ always denote random variables taken uniformly at random from A={1_,...,k_}. For all \(1\le i,j,\ell,m\le n\), we let<tbc>

\(U_{[i,j],[\ell,m]}=d_e(X_i\dots X_j,Y_\ell\dots,Y_m).\)

<tbc>Finally, we let \(V_n=min_{i\in\{0,\dots,n\}}U_{[1,i],[1,n-i]}\) and

\(\alpha'_k=lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]}{n}.\)

We will show that \(\alpha_k=2\alpha'_k\), and then explain how we compute bounds on \(\alpha'_k\).

### 2.1 From \(\alpha_k\) to \(\alpha'_k\)

We first prove that \(\alpha_k=2\alpha'_k\). The proof is directly inspired by the similar proof for \(\gamma_k\) in \[1\]. We will use the following special case of McDiarmid’s inequality \[15\].

**Theorem 1** (McDiarmid’s inequality)**.** _Let_ \(f:\mathcal{X}_1\times\mathcal{X}_2\times\cdots\times\mathcal{X}_m\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) _be a function with the property that changing any one argument of f while holding the others fixed changes the value of f by at most c. Consider independent random variables X_<sub>1</sub>_,...,X<sub>m</sub> where_ \(X_i\in\mathcal{X}_i\) _for all i. Then, for any_ \(\varepsilon>0\),<tbc>

\(\mathbb{P}\left[f(X_1,\dots,X_m)-\mathbb{E}\left[f(X_1,\dots,X_m)\right]\ge\varepsilon\right]\le exp\left(-\frac{2\varepsilon^2}{mc^2}\right),\)

<tbc>_and_<tbc>

\(\mathbb{P}\left[f(X_1,\dots,X_m)-\mathbb{E}\left[f(X_1,\dots,X_m)\right]\le-\varepsilon\right]\le exp\left(-\frac{2\varepsilon^2}{mc^2}\right).\)

We can apply this theorem to both _Vn_ and _Un_ with _m_=2_n_, _c_=1 and well-chosen values of \(\varepsilon\) that are going to be useful in what follows. **Lemma 2.** _For all n,_ \(\mathbb{P}\left[V_n\le\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]+\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}2}\right]\ge\frac{1}{2},\) (3) _and_ \(\mathbb{P}\left[U_n\ge\mathbb{E}\left[U_n\right]+\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}(4(n+1)^2)}\right]\le\frac{1}{4(n+1)^2}.\) (4) **Lemma 3.** _For all k,_ \(\alpha_k=2\alpha'_k.\) _Proof._ By definition, for all _n_, \(\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]}{n}\le\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[U_{\left[1,\lceil n/2\rceil\right],\left[1,\lceil n/2\rceil\right]}\right]}{n}\le\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[U_{\left[1,\lceil n/2\rceil\right],\left[1,\lceil n/2\rceil\right]}\right]}{\lceil n/2\rceil}\cdot\frac{\lceil n/2\rceil}{n}.\) The limit of the right-hand side as _n_ goes to infinity is \(\frac{\alpha_k}{2}\) which implies \(\alpha'_k\le\frac{\alpha_k}{2}\) . We now focus on proving \(\alpha'_k\ge\frac{\alpha_k}{2}\) . We have from (3), \(\frac{1}{2}\le\mathbb{P}\left[V_n\le\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]+\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}2}\right]\le\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbb{P}\left[U_{\left[1,i\right],\left[1,n-i\right]}\le\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]+\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}2}\right].\) Hence, there exists _i_ such that \(\mathbb{P}\left[U_{\left[1,i\right],\left[1,n-i\right]}\le\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]+\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}2}\right]\ge\frac{1}{2n}.\) Since _U_\[_i_+1_,n_\],\[_n-i_+1_,n_\] has the same distribution as _U_\[1_,i_\],\[1_,n-i_\], and they are independent of each others, we have \(\frac{1}{4n^2}\le\mathbb{P}\left[U_{\left[1,i\right],\left[1,n-i\right]}\le\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]+\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}2}\right]\cdot\mathbb{P}\left[U_{\left[i+1,n\right],\left[n-i+1,n\right]}\le\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]+\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}2}\right]\)
\(=\mathbb{P}\left[U_{\left[1,i\right],\left[1,n-i\right]}\le\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]+\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}2}\text{and}U_{\left[i+1,n\right],\left[n-i+1,n\right]}\le\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]+\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}2}\right]\)
\(\le\mathbb{P}\left[U_{\left[1,n\right],\left[1,n\right]}\le 2\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]+2\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}2}\right]\) From (4), \(\mathbb{P}\left[U_n\le\mathbb{E}\left[U_n\right]-\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}(4(n+1)^2)}\right]\le\frac{1}{4(n+1)^2}<\mathbb{P}\left[U_n\le 2\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]+2\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}2}\right],\) which implies \(\mathbb{E}\left[U_n\right]-\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}(4(n+1)^2)}\le 2\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]+2\sqrt{n\mathrm{log}2}.\) This implies \(\mathbb{E}\left[U_n\right]\le 2\mathbb{E}\left[V_n\right]+o(n)\). Taking the limit as _n_ goes to infinity, we get \(\alpha_k\le 2\alpha'_k\) which concludes the proof.

## 2.2 Bounds on \(\alpha'_k\) For any \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and, \(s,t\in\mathcal{A}^*\), we let \(V_n(s,t)=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{min}_{i+j=ni,j\ge 0}d_e(sX_1X_2\dots X_i,tY_1Y_2\dots Y_j)\right].\) As _n_ goes to infinity, the impact of the fixed prefixes _s_ and _t_ is negligible and the following Lemma is immediate. **Lemma 4.** _For any fixed_ \(s,t\in\mathcal{A}^*\)_, we have_ \(\alpha'_k=\mathrm{lim}_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{V_n(s,t)}{n}.\) We are now ready to bound \(\alpha'_k\) using this second expression. We let \(\vec{V_n}\) be the vector whose components are the _Vn(s,t_) where _s_ and _t_ range over all strings of length _h_ for a given _h_. Using the dynamic programming given earlier we provide upper bounds on the components of \(\vec{V_n}\) based on \(\vec{V_{n-1}}\) and \(\vec{V_{n-2}}\). **Fact 5.** _Let_ \(a\in\mathcal{A}\) _and_ \(s,t\in\mathcal{A}^*\)_, then_ \(V_n(as,at)\le\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|^2}\sum_{c,c^\prime\in\mathcal{A}}V_{n-2}(sc,tc').\) (5) _Proof._ We have \(V_n(as,at)=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{min}_{i+j=ni,j\ge 0}d_e(asx_1x_2\dots x_i,aty_1y_2\dots y_j)\right]\)
\(=\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{min}_{i+j=ni,j\ge 0}d_e(sx_1x_2\dots x_i,ty_1y_2\dots y_j)\right]\)
\(\le\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{min}_{i+j=ni,j\ge 1}d_e(sx_1x_2\dots x_i,ty_1y_2\dots y_j)\right]\)
\(=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|^2}\sum_{c,c^\prime\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{min}_{i+j=ni,j\ge 1}d_e(scx_2\dots x_i,tc'y_2\dots y_j)\right]\)
\(=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|^2}\sum_{c,c^\prime\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}\left[\mathrm{min}_{i+j=n-2i,j\ge 0}d_e(scx_1\dots x_i,tc'y_1\dots y_j)\right]\)
\(=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|^2}\sum_{c,c^\prime\in\mathcal{A}}V_{n-2}(sc,tc'),\) as desired.

**Fact 6.** _Let_ \(a,b\in\mathcal{A}\) _such that_ \(a\neq b\) _and_ \(s,t\in\mathcal{A}^*\)_, then_ \(V_n(as,bt)\le 1+\left\{\begin{array}{ c } \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{A}}V_{n-1}(sc,bt) \\ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{A}}V_{n-1}(as,tc) \\ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|^2}\sum_{c,c^\prime\in\mathcal{A}}V_{n-2}(sc,tc') \end{array}\right..\) _Proof._ We have \(V_n(as,bt)=\mathbb{E}\left[min_{i+j=ni,j\ge 0}d_e(asx_1x_2\dots x_i,bty_1y_2\dots y_j)\right]\)
\(=\mathbb{E}\left[min_{i+j=ni,j\ge 0}\left(1+min\left\{\begin{array}{ c } d_e(sx_1x_2\dots x_i,bty_1y_2\dots y_j) \\ d_e(asx_1x_2\dots x_i,ty_1y_2\dots y_j) \\ d_e(sx_1x_2\dots x_i,ty_1y_2\dots y_j) \end{array}\right)\right]\)
\(\le 1+min\left\{\begin{array}{ c } \mathbb{E}\left[min_{i+j=ni,j\ge 0}d_e(sx_1x_2\dots x_i,bty_1y_2\dots y_j) \\ \mathbb{E}\left[min_{i+j=ni,j\ge 0}d_e(asx_1x_2\dots x_i,ty_1y_2\dots y_j) \end{array}\right].\) We upper bound the first term of this minimum as follows, \(\mathbb{E}\left[min_{i+j=ni,j\ge 0}d_e(sx_1x_2\dots x_i,bty_1y_2\dots y_j)\right]\le\mathbb{E}\left[min_{i+j=ni\ge 1,j\ge 0}d_e(sx_1x_2\dots x_i,bty_1y_2\dots y_j)\right]\)
\(=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}\left[min_{i+j=ni\ge 1,j\ge 0}d_e(scx_2\dots x_i,bty_1y_2\dots y_j)\right]\)
\(=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{E}\left[min_{i+j=n-1i\ge 0,j\ge 0}d_e(scx_1\dots x_i,bty_1y_2\dots y_j)\right]\)
\(=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{A}}V_{n-1}(sc,bt).\) Similar computations for the two other terms of this minimum yields \(V_n(as,bt)\le 1+\left\{\begin{array}{ c } \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{A}}V_{n-1}(sc,bt) \\ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{A}}V_{n-1}(as,tc) \\ \frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|^2}\sum_{c,c^\prime\in\mathcal{A}}V_{n-2}(sc,tc') \end{array}\right.,\) as desired.

Let _T_ be the function given by these bounds such that \(\vec{V}_n\le T(V_{n-1}^\leftarrow,V_{n-2}^\leftarrow),\) (6) where \(\ge\) is taken component-wise. Moreover, _T_ is _translationally invariant_, that is, for all real _r_, \(T(\vec{v}+r,\vec{v}'+r)=T(v,v')+r,\) (7) where the sum of a vector with a real is taken component-wise. Finally, _T_ is also _monotonic_, that is, \(\vec{u}\le\vec{u}'\text{and}\vec{v}\le\vec{v}'\Longrightarrow T(u,v)\le T(u',v').\) (8) We are now ready to prove the main Lemma for the computation of \(\alpha'_k\). **Lemma 7.** _If there exists a vector_ \(\vec{v}\) _and a real r such that_ \(T(\vec{v},\vec{v}-r)\le\vec{v}+r,\) (9) _then there exists a real c such that_ \(\forall n\ge 0,\vec{V}_n\le\vec{v}+nr+c.\) (10) _In particular, this implies that_ \(\alpha'_k\le r\). _Proof._ We take any _c_ large enough such that (10) holds for \(n\in\{0,1\}\). We proceed by induction on _n_. The base case is covered by the choice of _c_. For the inductive step, assume that (10) holds for all _i\ \(\le T(\vec{v}+(n-1)r+c,\vec{v}+(n-2)r+c)\)
\(\le T(\vec{v},\vec{v}-r)+(n-1)r+c\)
\(\le\vec{v}+r+(n-1)r+c=\vec{v}+nr+c,\) which concludes our induction. ## 2.3 Implementation and bounds If we can find a vector \(\vec{v}\) and real _r_ satisfying (9), this implies \(\alpha_k\le 2r\). We use a computer program to verify the existence of such a vector. To find \(\vec{v}\) and _r_, we simply start with two vectors \(\vec{w}_0=\vec{w}_1=0\), and we iterate \(\vec{w}_n=T(w_{n-1}^\leftarrow,w_{n-2}^\leftarrow)\). It seems to be the case that \(\vec{w}_n-w_{n-1}^\leftarrow\) converges to a uniform vector, but we do not need to prove it. We simply take \(\vec{v}=w_n\) for some _n_ large enough, and we take _r_ to be the largest component of \(w_n-w_{n-1}+\varepsilon\). We then check that (9) is satisfied with this choice of \(\vec{v}\) and _r_. The implementation relies on fixed point arithmetic (that is, we fix some positive integer _p_, and we work with numbers of the form _a/p_ where \(a\in\mathbb{N}\)). We do all the rounding in the appropriate direction and in particular for the final step, we can formally verify with exact computation that (9) holds with the choice of \(\vec{v}\) and _r_.

In the implementation<sup>1</sup>, every pair of strings (_u,v_) is manipulated as the corresponding number _uv_ written in base _k_ (every considered pair is stored in a 64 bits integers). We also use the fact that a permutation of the alphabet does not change the result. That is, for every function _f_ that permutes the letters of the alphabet and for all strings _u,v_ of length _h,V<sub>n</sub>(u,v_)=_V<sub>n</sub>(f(u),f(v_)). For every pair _u,v_, we consider the _f_ that minimizes the string _uv_ for the lexicographic order (and we call _f(uv_) the _normalization_ of _uv_). This allows us to divide the size of the considered vector by ∼_k_!. However, it can be costly to recompute the renaming of the strings, so we provide three different versions of the code that provide different optimizations that are better for different values of _k_.

## The binary case.

A first version was written specifically for the binary alphabet. In this case, exchanging the letters of the string for the normalization is simply taking the bitwise negation of the string, and we can use bit-shifts and other bit manipulation to produce a faster code. In this code, the transformation _T_ is computed on the fly for every iteration, and we only store the vectors. The results obtained with this program are given in  2. The source code is in the file `EditDistance\_binary\_alphabet.cpp` from the GIT repository. This is the only version that uses parallelization (the optimal number of cores seems to be 2 as using more cores seems to increase considerably the number of cache misses).

We obtain \(\alpha_2\le 0.315514\). In \[14\], the author uses other symmetries that one might be able to adapt here to push the computations to _h_=18 instead of _h_=17 with the same machine (which, based on the difference between _h_=16 and _h_=17, would not improve the bound by much). Let us mention that the results obtained by Lueker have been very recently improved by optimizing the implementation and some of the techniques used might be applicable in our case as well \[11\].

## The general case.

The second version of the code precomputes the transformation _T_ and stores it. In the general setting of an alphabet of size _k_ the normalization is more costly to compute, so we only compute it once for every pair of strings. Storing _T_ increases the memory consumption (by a factor of order _k_), but saves a lot of computation time. The results obtained with this program are given in  3, and the source code is in the file `EditDistance\_general\_case.cpp` from the GIT repository.

<sup>1</sup>The code is available on `https://gite.lirmm.fr/mrosenfeld/expected-edit-distance`.

### Large alphabets.

In the third version we slightly change the data structure used to store the transformation _T_. This data structure uses maps instead of vectors and is more costly for small alphabets, but the cost is now linear in max(_k,_2_h_) instead of _k_ which means that for fixed _h_ we can compute a lower bound for very large values of _k_. The results obtained with this program are given in  4, and the source code is in the file `EditDistance\_ rally\_large\_alphabets.cpp` from the GIT repository.

## 3 Longest common subsequence

The technique that we use to compute bounds on \(\gamma_k\) is the same as in \[14\], and is moreover almost identical to what we did in the previous section. For the sake of completeness, we provide the definitions and the corresponding statement, but we do not repeat the proofs.

For any strings _u,v_, LCS(_u,v_) is the size of the longest common subsequence of _u_ and _v_. Remember, that given two strings \(u,v\in\mathcal{A}^*\), and letters \(a,b\in\mathcal{A}\), we have

\(\text{LCS}(au,bv)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
1+\text{LCS}(u,v) & \text{if}a=b \\
\text{max}(\text{LCS}(u,bv),\text{LCS}(au,v)) & \text{otherwise}
\end{array}\right.\) (11)

and for all _u_, \(\text{LCS}(u,\varepsilon)=\text{LCS}(\varepsilon,u)=0\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the empty string. For any strings \(u,v,u',v'\), we have

\(\text{LCS}(uv,u'v')\ge\text{LCS}(u,u')+\text{LCS}(v,v').\) (12)

For the rest of this section, the _X<sub>i</sub>_ and _Y<sub>i</sub>_ are independent uniform random variables from A={1_,...,k_}. For all _k_, the quantity \(\gamma_k\) is defined as

\(\gamma_k=lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[\text{LCS}(X_1\dots X_n,Y_1\dots Y_n)\right]}{n}.\)

Linearity of expectation and equation (12) imply that the sequence is subadditive which by Feketes’s lemma implies that \(\alpha_k\) is well-defined.

For any \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) and, \(s,t\in\mathcal{A}^*\), we let

\(W_n(s,t)=\mathbb{E}\left[min_{i+j=ni,j\ge 0}\text{LCS}(sX_1X_2\dots X_i,tY_1Y_2\dots Y_j)\right].\)

The following Lemma can be proven by following the same proof as for Lemma 4.

**Lemma 8.** _For any fixed_ \(s,t\in\mathcal{A}^*\)_, we have_

\(\gamma_k=lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{W_n(s,t)}{n}.\)

We let \(\vec{W}_n\) be the vector whose components are the _W<sub>n</sub>(s,t_) where _s_ and _t_ range over all strings of length _h_ for a given _h_. Equation (11) implies lower bounds on the components of \(\vec{W}_n\) based on \(W_{n-1}^{^\prime}\) and \(W_{n-2}^{^\prime}\).

**Fact 9.** _Let_ \(a\in\mathcal{A}\) _and_ \(s,t\in\mathcal{A}^*\)_, then_

\(W_n(as,at)\ge 1+\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|^2}\sum_{c,c^\prime\in\mathcal{A}}W_{n-2}(sc,tc').\) (13)

<tbc>**Fact 10.** _Let_ \(a,b\in\mathcal{A}\) _such that_ \(a\neq b\) _and_ \(s,t\in\mathcal{A}^*\)_, then_

\(W_n(as,bt)\ge\left\{\begin{array}{ c }
\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{A}}W_{n-1}(sc,bt) \\
\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{A}}W_{n-1}(as,tc)
\end{array}\right.\) (14)

Let _T_ be the function given by bounds (13) and (14) such that

\(\vec{W}_n\ge T(W_{n-1}^\leftarrow,W_{n-2}^\leftarrow),\)

where \(\ge\) is taken component-wise. We are now ready to state the main Lemma behind the computation of the upper bounds for \(\gamma_k\).

**Lemma 11.** _If there exists a vector_ \(\vec{w}\) _and real r such that_<tbc>

\(T(\vec{w},\vec{w}-r)\ge\vec{w}+r,\)

<tbc>_then there exists a real c such that_

\(\forall n\ge 0,\vec{W}_n\ge\vec{w}+nr+c.\)

_In particular, this implies that_ \(\gamma_k\ge 2r\).

On the other hand, it is known that \(\gamma_k\) behaves in \(2/\sqrt{k}+o(1/\sqrt{k})\) [13]. It is claimed in [2] that [6] contains a proof of \(\gamma_k\ge 1/\sqrt{k}\), but the only result in [6] that resembles this is \(\gamma_k\ge\frac{2k^2}{k^3+2k-1}\) . An explicit lower bound in \(\Theta(\sqrt{k})\) can probably be adapted from the asymptotic lower bound of [9]. Assuming that the claimed lower bound of \(\gamma_k\ge 1/\sqrt{k}\) is true, it is a better bound that what can be done with our software on modern machines for any \(k\ge k_0\) for some _k_<sub>0</sub> between 50 and 100.
